ask: Why is it on the path?
cards: The shortest day and longest night of the year has been marked since prehistory as the point when daylight begins to increase; Newgrange and Stonehenge are aligned with it.
Rome's festival of Saturn ran for seven days to 23 December, with a public banquet, gift-giving, gambling and masters serving their slaves at table.
The pre-Christian religion of Scandinavia worshipped Odin, Thor, Freyr and Freyja with sacrifices and feasts led by chieftains and kings.
Feasting, ceremonial drinking and oath swearing were central to this Germanic winter festival, which merged with Christmas and still names it in Northern European languages.
Slavic rulers adopted Christianity between 863 and 988, but popular resistance lasted for centuries and the old rites lived on in a “double faith”.
The Slavic name for the days from Christmas to Epiphany covers rituals of which some date to pre-Christian times, among them carols sung from house to house for gifts.
On the longest night of the year families in Iran and its neighbours gather to eat, drink and read Hafez; in Zoroastrian tradition the night was inauspicious.
Punjab marks the passing of the winter solstice with bonfires, festive foods, bhangra and songs of Dulla Bhatti on the night before Makar Sankranti.
China's winter solstice festival, first celebrated under the Zhou and made official under the Han, reads the lengthening days through yin and yang.
Japan closes the year with house cleaning, repaid debts and long noodles, and at midnight most Buddhist temples strike a large bell 108 times.
